routes.description: Show that Catholic theism can reconcile hiddenness, uneven religious geography, sincere nonbelief, hell, suffering, and original sin with universal grace, providence, differentiated creation, and meaningful creaturely agency.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by establishing universal sufficient grace, a coherent role for free reception or refusal across a temporally extended life, morally relevant providential differentiation, and a non-punitive account of inherited deprivation and restoration.

motionBridge.description: Catholic theism must provide a unified account on which the disputed phenomena remain compatible with divine goodness, justice, universal salvific will, and creaturely agency.

centralBridges.description: Establish that grace and access to God are universally sufficient even when their historical, cultural, experiential, and intellectual mediation differs.
Explain how recurrent providential opportunities can operate without compelling assent and how meaningful creaturely acceptance or resistance remains possible.
Show why differentiated natural and supernatural gifts need not constitute injustice or divine favoritism within a gratuitous and communally ordered creation.
Account for original sin as deprivation of superadded grace rather than inherited personal guilt, while preserving responsibility and personal availability of restoration.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how patience, inquiry, questioning, and suffering may progressively form a person's capacity to recognize revelation across a life.
Defend the theological and canonical interpretive framework required for the accounts of the Fall, Job, providence, and divine questioning.

routes.description: Show that persistent sincere nonbelief, culturally patterned religious access, eternal consequences, morally troubling suffering, and inherited deprivation are less expected under Catholic claims about divine love, justice, grace, and providence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by establishing genuine nonresistant seeking, materially unequal access and arbitrary contingencies, inadequacies in free-rejection explanations, and unresolved injustice in hell, suffering, or original sin.

motionBridge.description: The skeptical route must connect the disputed phenomena to a substantive evidential or moral conflict with Catholic theism's claims about God, grace, providence, and salvation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that religious belief tracks geography and social transmission in a way more readily expected from human cultural production than universal divine outreach.
Establish that capable and persistent seekers can remain involuntarily unconvinced despite a purportedly powerful divine desire for relationship.
Show that eternal outcomes tied to cognition, social encounters, lifespan, or providentially arranged circumstances remain arbitrary, unfair, or incompatible with freedom.
Show that deception, deficient understanding, and lack of personal participation undermine culpability for the Fall and the justice of inherited consequences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether a person who adequately understood the supreme good and eternal loss could rationally and culpably reject salvation.
Test whether formative or canonical interpretations of suffering adequately reconcile divine silence and scriptural depictions with love and compassion.

sections.title: Religious Geography and Mediated Access
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether culturally uneven belief is compatible with universally sufficient grace or instead supports a sociological explanation of religious distribution.

sections.title: Sincere Nonbelief and Developing Receptivity
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether persistent seekers receive adequate divine access and whether delayed recognition across a life can explain apparent silence.

sections.title: Freedom, Providence, and Eternal Consequences
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether noncompelling grace and creaturely refusal coherently ground salvation outcomes without making them arbitrary, cognitively impaired, or providentially determined.

sections.title: Justice, Unequal Gifts, and Creaturely Goods
sections.rationale: This issue addresses the governing standard of divine justice and whether unequal natural, supernatural, and experiential goods can serve a gratuitous communal order.

sections.title: Original Sin, Culpability, and Inherited Deprivation
sections.rationale: This issue tests the origin, transmission, and consequences of the Fall, including deception, representation, lost grace, inherited responsibility, and restoration.
